intro: Optimize PDF for web linearises the document: it reorders its objects so that everything needed to display the first page sits at the start of the file. When someone opens the PDF from a link, the browser can show the cover while the rest is still downloading, instead of waiting for the whole file. Some readers call this “fast web view”.

It is useful for catalogues, annual reports, restaurant menus or manuals you publish on your site and that weigh several megabytes. Linearisation is done with qpdf and changes nothing you can see: text, images, links and bookmarks stay the same.

Linearising does not reduce the size; it may even add a few kilobytes for the extra tables. If you also want the file lighter, turn on “Compress first” under more options: the balanced level of Compress PDF is applied and that version is only used if it is smaller than the original.
For progressive loading to work, the server that hosts the PDF has to support range requests, which almost every current web server and content delivery network does.

faq.q: How do I know whether a PDF is already linearised?
faq.a: Many readers show it in the document properties, for example as “Fast Web View: Yes”. Linearising it again does no harm.
Not for an attachment, because the whole file is downloaded before it opens. For that, Compress PDF is the better choice.

faq.q: Can I optimise several PDFs at once?
faq.a: Yes. Each one comes out with the suffix “-web” and, if you upload more than one, you also get a ZIP with all of them.

faq.q: What if the PDF has a password?
faq.a: This tool does not ask for a password. If the file needs one to open, unlock it first with Unlock PDF and, if needed, protect it again once it is optimised.
